The diﬀerent status of diﬀerent workshops often exists in the distributed manufacturing mode, called as the heterogeneous work- shops. This distributed manufacturing mode brings new challenges to shop scheduling. Introduction In this work we deal with a parallel machine scheduling prob- lem with setup times depending not only on the sequence of jobs, but also on all the machine setups that have been already done, for minimizing the sum of the completion times of all jobs. Several performance measures are used to evaluate the quality of a scheduling. The most common criteria are the minimization of the maximum completion time (makespan), the minimization of the total completion time (TCT), and the minimization of some kind of tardiness. In particular, the minimization of the TCT is a cri- terion that contributes to the maximization of the production ﬂow, the minimization of the work-in-process inventories, and balanced usage of resources ( Xiong, Xing, Wang, Lei, & Han, 2014 ). Problem description In this paper, we address the job shop scheduling problem with ﬂexible machines and sequence-dependent setup times. Scheduling refers to the allocation of resources to perform a set of tasks over a period of time. Under economic and commercial market pressures, developing an eﬃcient and accurate schedule becomes increasingly important. Due to the wide applicability for real-world manufac- turing systems, the Job shop Scheduling Problem (JSP) is one of the most popular scheduling problems. In the classical JSP, a set of jobs are to be processed on a set of given machines. Each job can be di- vided into operations, which are assigned to prescribed machines, and are processed according to speciﬁc technological orders. Considering the growing demand on ﬂexibility and reliability, several machines are often capable of performing similar tasks. Es- pecially in Flexible Manufacturing Systems (FMS), a high machine ﬂexibility is characteristic ( Rossi, 2014 ). In this context, the avail- ability of alternative resources can increase performance, and help to manage preventive maintenance or tackle breakdown and other unforeseen events. Taking this into account, the JSP can be ex- tended to the Flexible Job shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP), where ∗Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: liji.shen@whu.edu (L. Shen), dauzere-peres@emse.fr (S. Dauzère-Pérès). an operation can be carried out on a set of compatible machines. The FJSP was originally stated by Brucker and Schlie (1990) . The routing ﬂexibility of a job then results in two sub-problems: The assignment of each operation to a speciﬁc machine has to be de- cided and operations have to be sequenced on each machine to optimize a given criterion. Moreover, setup times are another important characteristic of many practical real-world scheduling settings. The integration of setup times has a signiﬁcant impact on the applicability and per- formance of scheduling algorithms for practical manufacturing sys- tems (e.g., Krajewski, King, Ritzman, & Wong, 1987; Wilbrecht & Prescott, 1969 ). Undeniable savings have also been observed when setup times are explicitly investigated in the scheduling decisions ( Allahverdi, Ng, Cheng, & Kovalyov, 2008 ). Conventional studies of manufacturing lines, however, often focus on the operation time, and setup times are assumed to be zero or constant. In many real applications such as chemical, printing, pharmaceutical, and auto- mobile manufacturing, setups are not only required between jobs but also strongly depend on the preceding process on the same machine. These facts motivate our study. More precisely, we consider the ﬂexible job shop schedul- ing problem with sequence-dependent setup times (FJSP-SDST) to minimize the makespan. Sequence dependency indicates that the magnitude of setup times is determined by the current job as well as the direct previous job processed on the same machine. As a generalization of the classical JSP, the FJSP-SDST is known to be strongly NP-hard ( Garey, Johnson, & Sethi, 1976 ). Introduction Scheduling is the allocation of resources to perform a set of tasks over a period of time. Most scheduling problems are complex com- binatorial optimization problems and they are mainly very difﬁcult to solve. One of the most difﬁcult problems in this area is the ﬂex- ible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP). The FJSP is an extension of the classical job shop scheduling problem (JSP), which provides a closer approximation to a wide range of scheduling problems encountered in real manufacturing systems. In this problem, oper- ations are allowed to be processed on any among a set of available machines. The problem is to assign each operation to an appropri- ate machine, and to sequence the operations on the machines in order to minimize the performance indicator. There are considerable numbers of practical assumptions in the real world scheduling settings. One of the most widely used assumptions in the real scheduling settings is the consideration of sequence-dependent setup times (SDST). The motivation behind this assumption stems from the fact that there are tremendous savings when setup times are explicitly included in the schedul- ing decisions [1]. The conventional studies of manufacturing lines often assumed that the total time to perform a set of manufacturing ∗Corresponding author. The majority of such research focused on the ‘operation’ time, time of pure value-adding processes; such conventional research usually assumed that the time spent between two tasks was zero, or the setup times were constant regardless of task order. How- ever, some research has shown that, in many real situations, task sequences signiﬁcantly affect the sizes of setup times [2]. Consid- ering this assumption, not only setup times are not counted as a trivial part of processing times, but are also separately studied as an effective factor in operation scheduling. In many real-life situ- ations such as chemical, printing, pharmaceutical, and automobile manufacturing [3], the setup operations, such as cleaning up or changing tools, are not only often required between jobs but are also strongly dependent on the immediately preceding process on the same machine [4,5] (sequence-dependent). In this paper, we study the ﬂexible job-shop scheduling with sequence-dependent setup times (hereinafter referred to as SDST- FJSP). In general, the FJSP is strongly NP-hard and too intractable to be solved by exact methods. It is obvious that the SDST-FJSP is more complex than the FJSP. The high complexity level of the SDST-FJSP justiﬁes the need for efﬁcient methods to obtain approx- imate solutions of high quality (optimal or near optimal schedule) in a reasonable computational time. Introduction The general job shop scheduling problem (JSP) was introduced to deal with the sequencing decisions of manufacturing operations in low volume-high variety manufacturing systems in which part routes are ﬁxed while differ considerably from one part to the other. With the advent of ﬂexible manufacturing systems (FMSs), it became necessary to relax the assumption of ﬁxed part routes in order to be able to deal with the arising scheduling problems in these systems. FMSs are characterized by the existence of general purpose computer numerically controlled (CNC) machines that can perform various types of manufacturing operations. This made it possible for a manufacturing operation of a given part to be conducted on any of a set of different machines with possibly different processing times. This means that the operations’ routing became a decision variable instead of being ﬁxed. In the 1980s, the ﬂexible job shop scheduling problem (FJSP) was introduced to address this situation. The FJSP, denoted FJc|rcrc| according to the three-ﬁeld notation in [1], is composed of two interacting problems. The ﬁrst is concerned with selecting a machine for each operation, and the second is a regular JSP with possible recirculation, i.e. a given part may visit the same machine more than once. As indicated in [2], there are two approaches that are followed in dealing with this problem. The ﬁrst is a hierarchical or a decomposition approach which solves the machine assignment problem ﬁrst; and based on its solution, a JSP is formulated and solved. The second is a concurrent one which looks for a solution to both problems simultaneously. Early studies of the FJSP developed both hierarchical and concurrent approaches that are based on mixed integer linear programming (MILP) models and dispatching rules [3–6]. To address this complex problem efficiently, this paper proposes an Enhanced Graphical Method (EGM), which integrates both scheduling stages within a unified graphical framework, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional approaches that treat the two stages separately. The EGM framework consists of four core modules: initial solution generation, graphical search, local search, and acceptance criteria. In the graphical search phase, two key enhancements are proposed. First, a bidirectional shifting mechanism is developed to construct an obstacle graph by left or right shifting the remaining operations, significantly expanding the neighborhood solution space. Second, a layered path planning algorithm based on non-dominated sorting is introduced to improve the search efficiency. Furthermore, three neighborhood structures are designed within the graphical framework to support integrated scheduling of job allocation and operation sequencing. In the local search phase, a dynamic tabu search mechanism is incorporated to optimize the scheduling of critical factories, further enhancing solution quality and stability. The proposed EGM was evaluated on 210 Taillard benchmark instances. Experimental results demonstrate that EGM consistently outperforms four state-of-the-art algorithms in both solution quality and robustness, especially by discovering the upper bounds of 71 benchmark instances. 1. Introduction The modern manufacturing industry faces dual challenges: increas­ ingly personalized customer demands and heightened market volatility. Traditional centralized production often suffers from inflexible resource assignments and slow reaction speeds, making it difficult to deliver the agility demanded by fast-changing environments (Behnamian & Fatemi Ghomi, 2016). In response, distributed manufacturing has been pro­ posed as an effective alternative: by coordinating production across geographically dispersed facilities, it shortens supply chain response times while optimizing spatial resource distribution, thus reducing transportation energy consumption and operational risks. However, the rise of distributed manufacturing has also introduced new challenges in scheduling research. Among them, the Distributed Job Shop Scheduling Problem (DJSP) is a representative and complex issue. DJSP can be defined as the problem of assigning n jobs to f factories, involving two interrelated scheduling decisions: (1) assigning jobs to factories and (2) scheduling operations within each factory, the latter corresponding to the classic Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSP). Although there are relatively mature research results on JSP, studies focusing on how to effectively assign jobs to factories and achieve coordinated optimization across the two stages remain limited, leaving significant room for improvement. Existing studies on job-to-factory assignment can be broadly classi­ fied into three categories. The first is static assignment strategies, such as the load-balancing method proposed by S¸ahman (2021), where jobs are bound to specific factories during initial solution construction. Once assigned, jobs cannot be reallocated, limiting the algorithm to a single, fixed combination of assignments. The second category involves dy­ namic assignment during the search process. For example, Chaouch et al. (2019) integrated job allocation mechanisms into an ant colony optimization algorithm, dynamically assigning some jobs to factories with the lowest current load. The mixed-integer linear programming model (MILP) of the DHFSP is established, where different time-of-use electricity prices and states of machines (running and idle) are integrated. Introduction This study concerns the no-wait job-shop scheduling problem (NWJSP) with the objective of minimizing makespan among all jobs, which can be denoted as the triplet J nwt C | | m max, where Jm denotes a machine environment that is a job-shop with m machines; nwt indicates the job-shop scheduling problem with the no-wait constraint, and Cmax indicates that the objective is to minimize the makespan. The NWJSP is an extension of the classical job-shop scheduling problem (JSP) under the no-wait constraint, which arises when the characteristics of process technology or the absence of storage capacity requires that consecutive operations in any job are processed one after another without waiting. The J nwt C | | m max problem, addressed herein, arises in several industries, including steel production, chemical and pharmaceutical manufacture, semiconductor testing, computer system development and the produc- tion of concrete wares (Zhu & Li, 2012; Sundar, Suganthan, Jin, Xiang, & Soon, 2017). Given the complexities of the J nwt C | | m max problem, ef- ficient heuristics are needed to help generate dependable solutions for practical industrial-scale applications. Although this problem has wide industrial applications, much less attention has been paid to it than has been paid to the classical JSP. This study’s review of the limited studies in the literature suggests that there is room for further improving the quality of solutions to facilitate industrial applications of this emerging scheduling problem. This is the primary motivation for this study. To the best of our knowledge, Hall and Sriskandarajah (1996) were the first to summarize research on the NWJSP. Allahverdi (2016) comprehensively surveyed the literature on the J nwt C | | m max problem. Since the J nwt C | | m max problem is NP-hard in the strong sense (Bansal, Mahdian, & Sviridenko, 2005) when each job has at least three op- erations, it does not has a polynomial-time approximation scheme, unless = P NP. Typically, the stafﬁng level (ratio of operators to machines) is less than 100%, where workers (opera- tors) are transferred from one task (machine) to another as needed; usually subject to certain limitations such as: batch size, worker’s idle time, delivery due dates, queue length, and upfront training (e.g., Bokhorst, Slomp, & Gaalman, 2006; Kher, Malhotra, Phili- poom, & Fry, 1999; Treleven, 1989). Cross-training allows the workers to share workloads amongst themselves within any given team conﬁguration (McCreery, Krajewski, Leong, & Ward, 2004). A cross-trained workforce is believed to offer several beneﬁts to ﬁrms. It can help the ﬁrm respond to unexpected and unbalanced workloads by reducing manufacturing lead-times and inventories of work-in-process, accelerating the learning process of workers, improving quality and productivity and enhancing customer ser- vice (e.g., Felan & Fry, 2001; Krajewski, King, Ritzman, & Wong, 1987; Treleven, 1989), as well as reducing fatigue, boredom or repetitive stress (e.g., Hopp, Tekin, & Van Oyen, 2004). There has been considerable investigation of DRC systems and this literature can be clustered into three groups, which are brieﬂy surveyed below. The ﬁrst group of studies investigated the use of analytical mod- els including mathematical, queuing and scheduling models in order to ﬁnd optimal or near optimal solutions to questions regard- ing the degree of ﬂexibility and the assignment (e.g., where and when to transfer) of the workforce (e.g., Bobrowski & Park, 1993; Fryer, 1976; Hottenstein & Bowman, 1998; Inman, Jordan, & Blu- menfeld, 2004; Nelson, 1967; Treleven & Elvers, 1985). Introduction Multi-objective optimization problems (MOPs) are character- ized by multiple objectives to be optimized concurrently [1]. Due to the conflicts between objectives in MOP, there is nearly no single solution that can satisfy all the objectives at the same time. Therefore, the goal of solving an MOP is to find a set of Pareto nondominated solutions that entail the tradeoff between different objectives [2]. The set of all Pareto nondominated solutions is called the Pareto optimal set (PS), and the mapping of PS in the objective space is called the Pareto front (PF) [1]. When solving an MOP, the obtained solutions in PS should not only converge to the true PF of the optimized MOP as close as possible, but also distribute on the PF as evenly as possible. Generally, convergence and diversity are two critical criteria for evaluating the quality of the final solutions [3]. Introduction Automatic algorithm design (AAD) has shown to be able to produce state-of-the-art algorithms for the permutation flowshop problem [43]. In particular, the EMILI framework allows the definition of both high specialized problem-specific components as well as general problem-agnostic components. The permutation flowshop problem (PFSP) is a very well known problem [14]. It has been shown to be NP -hard for different objectives with the exception of the two machine case for the makespan objective [23]. The problem models a flowshop where a set of jobs have to be processed on a group of machines. Several additional constraints have been proposed in the literature to take into account different scenarios. Often, machines have to be set up before being able to process a job. For instance, a machine may need to be cleaned or calibrated before pro­ cessing another job. The setup time may depend not only on the job that has to be processed, but also on the changes made to the setup of the machine before processing the previous job. The permutation flowshop problem with sequence dependent setup times, PFSPsdst, has been introduced to model this scenario. Introduction Scheduling deals with the allocation of resources to tasks over time to optimize one or more objectives ( Pinedo, 2016 ). The job- shop scheduling problem is one of the most well-known ( Bowman, 1959 ) and diﬃcult ( Gonzalez & Sahni, 1978 ) scheduling problems in the literature. In a job-shop scheduling problem, a set of jobs must be processed on a set of machines, and each job requires a sequence of operations (a route) before being completed. A ma- chine can only perform one operation at a time, and preemption is not allowed. Each operation can only be performed on a spec- iﬁed machine while, in the ﬂexible job-shop scheduling problem, operations can be assigned to multiple machines. Such problems and their extensions can model a wide range of real-world appli- cations, for example in the contexts of healthcare ( Pham & Klink- ert, 2008 ), manufacturing ( Tamssaouet et al., 2022 ) and transport ( Lamorgese & Mannino, 2019 ). This explains why so much research has been conducted on designing exact and heuristic algorithms to solve these problems. ∗Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: karim.tamssaouet@bi.no (K. Tamssaouet), stephane.dauzere- peres@bi.no (S. Dauzère-Pérès) . Job-shop scheduling problems are computationally intractable when dealing with large instances. Therefore, heuristic algorithms are considered in practice to ﬁnd good quality solutions in reason- able computational times. It is common to differentiate between constructive and improvement heuristics. A constructive heuristic builds a solution from scratch, often by using some greedy crite- ria. An improvement heuristic, starting from one or a set of initial solutions generated randomly or by some constructive heuristic, it- eratively explores the search space to obtain better solutions. Lo- cal search algorithms are a broad class of improvement algorithms where, at each iteration, an improving solution is found by search- ing the neighborhood of the current solution, that is, a set of solu- tions that are, in some sense, “close” to that solution. Therefore, to derive a local search algorithm for an optimization problem, one must carefully deﬁne the neighborhood structure specifying the neighborhood to explore for each solution. Typically, a neighbor- hood structure is not deﬁned by explicitly enumerating the set of possible neighbors, but rather implicitly by deﬁning the possible local changes, called moves , to apply to the current solution. Introduction The classical job shop (JS) problem is a diﬃcult combinatorial optimization problem that has been widely studied. A set of jobs have to be executed on a set of machines, where each job is de- ﬁned as a sequence of operations, and each operation speciﬁes the machine on which it has to be processed. A machine can process at most one job operation at a time, a processing time is deﬁned for each operation and, once started, an operation cannot be in- terrupted (non-preemptive). The goal is to ﬁnd a a particular se- quencing of operations on each of the machines and a schedule (i.e. start time for each operation) for the sequencing that mini- mizes an objective function. A number of possible objectives have been investigated for the classical job shop problem. A prominent one is makespan minimization, where the time it takes to com- pletely service all job operations has to be minimized. One of the assumptions in the classical JS problem is that as soon as an operation ﬁnishes executing on a machine, the machine becomes available. Basically, this means that there exists a buffer to store the job (product) between successive operations, and that this buffer has suﬃcient capacity to store all partially serviced jobs. ∗Corresponding author E-mail addresses: jmogali@andrew.cmu.edu (J.K. Mogali), laurabar@andrew.cmu.edu (L. Barbulescu), ssmith@andrew.cmu.edu (S.F. Smith). In most real-world settings this is not a realistic expectation as there may be physical limits on the capacity of the buffer. Differ- ent versions of the job shop problem have been deﬁned in the lit- erature, to include more realistic features in the problem formula- tion. Introduction Many natural processes have evolved to match their environment; this instinctive behavior demonstrates a level of intelligence. Nature- inspired intelligence forms the foundation of metaheuristic algorithms, which are broadly employed to tackle real-world problems. The Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [1] is a prime example of metaheuristics inspired by the principles of swarm intelligence. PSO mimics the posi­ tional updates and velocity adjustment instincts of bird flocks—the so-called foraging behaviors—to establish a balance between global and local search strategies in the pursuit of optimal solutions. PSO falls into the category of population-based, stochastic metaheuristic algorithms and is widely used for solving optimization problems [2]. As one of the well-established categories of optimization problems, scheduling provides decision support for short-term planning under limited resources and operational constraints at the shop-floor level. Basic scheduling problems can often be solved by employing exact methods and dynamic programming algorithms that are embedded in commercial solvers. However, more complex mathematical models are high-dimensional and often suffer from long computation times or an inability to find an optimal solution [3]. This reduces the usefulness and limits industrial applicability of such complex optimization problems. Our preliminary investigations showed that over 1300 peer- reviewed research works in scheduling have applied PSO. Despite its merits—including robustness, strong distributed capabilities, and ease of implementation and hybridization [2]–PSO faces challenges such as premature convergence and entrapment in local optimality, which are mainly attributed to the increasing complexity of optimization problems across different application domains [4–7]. A considerable number of existing research works have contributed to addressing these inherent limitations of PSO. The rapid expansion of PSO’s applications highlights the need for a systematic, algorithm-focused review. The current literature lacks a comprehensive review of these contributions across the entire spectrum of scheduling problems. Synthesizing PSO’s developments may pave the way for further advancements. From the existing studies, Menos- Aikateriniadis et al. [8] is the most relevant review, where PSO algo­ rithms are used for energy scheduling in the context of demand response provision for power distribution networks. Their survey is limited to a narrow context, whereas scheduling has diverse applications ranging from project management and healthcare to production planning, en­ ergy management, cloud computing, transport and educational time­ tabling. Besides, their manual review did not draw a big picture of PSO’s computational developments. To our best knowledge, there is no algorithm-based, interpretive literature analysis of PSO studies that re­ views the most important extensions across the entire scheduling domain. Introduction Optimization problems can be divided into continuous optimization problems (CnOPs) and discrete optimization problems (DOPs) accord- ing to the category of the decision variables. In the fast few years, lots of algorithms have been proposed to address CnOPs or DOPs. However, many real-world optimization problems not only involve continuous but discrete variables, e.g., industrial design problems and ﬁnancial opti- mization problems, which are called Mixed-Variable Optimization Prob- lems (MVOPs). The mixed variables deﬁnitely increase the complexity of the search space and improve the diﬃculty of solving these optimization problems. Therefore, it is necessary to design more eﬃcient algorithms to solve MVOPs. Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are a new kind of optimization algo- rithms that do not rely on the mathematical characteristic of the prob- lems, e.g., Genetic Algorithm (GA) [12] , Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [34] , Diﬀerential Evolution (DE) [36] and Ant Colony Optimiza- tion (ACO) [8] . The classical JSP consists of scheduling a set of jobs on a set of machines, subject to the constraint that each job has a speciﬁed processing order throughout. JSP is an NP-hard problem (Garey et al., 1976), so different heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms are considered for solving JSP. The ﬂexible job-shop problem (FJSP) is an extension of the job-shop problem that allows an operation to be processed by any machine from a given set along different routes. Some applications of FJSP are in planning ﬂexible manufacturing systems (FMS), chemical materi- als processing plants, and transportation systems. In addition to the common complexities inherent of JSP, the ﬂexible job-shop problem poses an even greater complexity due to the need to determine the assignment of operations to machines. The FJS problem consists of two sub-problems of routing and scheduling. The routing sub-problem assigns each operation to a machine among a set of machines authorized for each job. The scheduling sub-problem involves sequencing the operations assigned to the machines in order to obtain a feasible schedule that minimizes a predeﬁned objective. Brucker and Schlie (1990) were the ﬁrst to address the FJSP. They proposed a polynomial algorithm for solving the FJSP with two jobs, in which the machines capable of performing one operation have the same processing time. For solving problems with more than two jobs, different hierarchical and integrated approaches have been used. According to hierarchical approaches, assigning operations to machines and their sequencing on the machines are accomplished independently from each other whereas in integrated approaches, the two tasks are jointly accomplished. Hierarchical approaches are based on the idea of decomposing the original problem in order to reduce its complexity. Brandi- marte (1993) was the ﬁrst to use decomposition for the FJSP. He solved the routing sub-problem using some existing dispatching rules and then focused on the scheduling sub-problem, which is solved using a tabu search heuristic. Tung et al. (1999) developed a similar approach for scheduling a ﬂexible manufacturing system. Mati et al. (2001) proposed a greedy heuristic to deal simultaneously with assigning and sequencing sub-problems of the ﬂexible job-shop model. Introduction Job-shop scheduling problem (JSP), which is among the hardest combinatorial optimization problems (Sonmez & Baykasoglu, 1998), is a branch of production scheduling. It is well known that this problem is NP-hard (Garey, Johnson, & Sethi, 1976). The clas- sical JSP schedules a set of jobs on a set of machines with the objec- tive to minimize a certain criterion, subjected to the constraint that each job has a speciﬁed processing order through all machines which are ﬁxed and known in advance. Flexible job-shop problem (FJSP) is an extension of the classical JSP that allows one operation which can be processed on one machine out of a set of alternative machines. It is closer to the real manufacturing situation. Because of the additional needs to deter- mine the assignment of operations on the machines, FJSP is more complex than JSP, and incorporates all the difﬁculties and com- plexities of JSP. The problem of scheduling jobs in FJSP could be decomposed into two sub-problems: a routing sub-problem, which is assigning each operation to a machine out of a set of capable machines and a scheduling sub-problem, which is sequencing the assigned operations on all selected machines in order to obtain a feasible schedule with optimized objectives (Xia & Wu, 2005). The scheduling problem in a ﬂexible job shop is at least as hard as the job shop problem, which is considered one of the most dif- ﬁcult problems in combinatorial optimization (Lawler, Lenstra, Rinnooy Kan, & Shmoys, 1993). Although an optimal solution algo- rithm for the classical JSP has not been developed yet, there is a trend in the research community to model and solve much more complex version of the FJSP (Baykasoglu, Ozbakir, & Sonmez, 2004). The research on the multi-objective FJSP is much less than the mono-objective FJSP. Brandimarte (1993) was the ﬁrst to apply the decomposition approach into the FJSP. He solved the routing sub-problem by using some existing dispatching rules and then focused on the scheduling sub-problem, which was solved by using a tabu search heuristic. Hurink, Jurisch, and Thole (1994) proposed a tabu search heuristic. They considered the reassign- ment and rescheduling as two different types of moves. The most important issue in employing meta-heuristics for combinatorial optimization problems is to de- velop an effective ‘‘problem mapping” and ‘‘solution generation” mechanism.
